title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
This assignment analyzes MaxDiff (Best-Worst Scaling) survey data collected from MSBA students at UCSD Rady to estimate relative preferences across the 10 core MSBA courses.
MaxDiff works by showing each respondent a small subset of items (4 at a time) and asking them to pick the most preferred and least preferred item in that subset. They repeat this over many screens. The key advantage over a 1–10 rating scale is that humans are much better at comparative judgments than at calibrating a numeric scale consistently. MaxDiff forces real trade-offs and avoids scale-use bias — no more everyone rating everything a 7.
We estimate preferences three ways:

Counts analysis — the percentage of times each class was picked best minus the percentage of times it was picked worst. Simple and fast to communicate.
MNL via Maximum Likelihood — the multinomial logit model fit by optimizing the log-likelihood. Gives point estimates and standard errors.
MNL via Bayesian (MCMC) — the same model fit by Metropolis-Hastings sampling. Gives full posterior distributions and easy uncertainty on derived quantities.

The three methods should broadly agree on the ranking. They differ in how they handle uncertainty and how much information they extract from the data.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Counts Analysis
The counts analysis is the simplest way to summarize MaxDiff data. For each class \(j\), we compute what fraction of times it was shown it was picked best, and what fraction it was picked worst. The score is:
\[\text{score}_j = \%\text{best}_j - \%\text{worst}_j\]
A score near +1 means students almost always chose this class as the best option when they saw it. A score near −1 means it was almost always chosen as worst. A score near 0 is middle-of-the-pack (or polarizing). This method is transparent and easy to explain, but it does not model the choice process — it ignores the competitive context of which other items were shown alongside each class.


Code
times_shown  = df.groupby("item").size()
times_best   = df[df["response"] ==  1].groupby("item").size()
times_worst  = df[df["response"] == -1].groupby("item").size()

counts = pd.DataFrame({
    "times_shown": times_shown,
    "times_best":  times_best.reindex(times_shown.index, fill_value=0),
    "times_worst": times_worst.reindex(times_shown.index, fill_value=0),
}).reset_index()

counts["pct_best"]  = counts["times_best"]  / counts["times_shown"]
counts["pct_worst"] = counts["times_worst"] / counts["times_shown"]
counts["score"]     = counts["pct_best"] - counts["pct_worst"]
counts = counts.merge(labels, on="item")
counts = counts.sort_values("score", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
counts["counts_rank"] = range(1, 11)

display_df = counts[["counts_rank","short_name","times_shown","times_best","times_worst",
                      "pct_best","pct_worst","score"]].copy()

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
section: From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
text:
From MaxDiff Data to MNL Choices
Before fitting the MNL, we need to think about how a MaxDiff task converts into standard discrete-choice observations.
In a typical MNL setup, a person sees \(J\) options and picks one. The model assigns each option \(j\) a utility \(\beta_j\) and says the probability of choosing \(j\) from a set \(\mathcal{S}\) is the softmax:
\[P(\text{best} = j \mid \mathcal{S}) = \frac{\exp(\beta_j)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{S}} \exp(\beta_k)}\]
Each MaxDiff task gives two MNL observations:

The best pick from all 4 shown items — standard softmax over the full set.
The worst pick from the remaining 3 items after removing the best. Because picking the minimum utility item is equivalent to picking the maximum of the negated utilities, this is just another MNL with \(-\beta\):

\[P(\text{worst} = j \mid \mathcal{S} \setminus \{j^*_b\}) = \frac{\exp(-\beta_j)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{S} \setminus \{j^*_b\}} \exp(-\beta_k)}\]
Identifiability: The softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all \(\beta\)’s, so only \(J-1 = 9\) parameters are identified. We fix \(\beta_1 = 0\) (item 1 = AI Math/Prog as reference) and estimate \(\beta_2, \ldots, \beta_{10}\). All estimates are interpreted relative to item 1.


Code
tasks_list = []
for (rid, t), group in df.groupby(["record_id", "task"]):
    br = group[group["response"] ==  1]
    wr = group[group["response"] == -1]
    if len(br) == 1 and len(wr) == 1:
        tasks_list.append({
            "items": list(group["item"].values),
            "best":  int(br["item"].values[0]),
            "worst": int(wr["item"].values[0]),
        })

tasks_df = pd.DataFrame(tasks_list)

items_arr = np.array(tasks_df["items"].tolist()) - 1
best_arr  = np.array(tasks_df["best"].tolist())  - 1
worst_arr = np.array(tasks_df["worst"].tolist()) - 1

print(f"Total tasks for likelihood: {len(tasks_df)}")
print("\nFirst 3 tasks:")
print(tasks_df.head(3).to_string(index=False))

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Maximum Likelihood
The log-likelihood sums two contributions per task: the log-probability of the best pick, and the log-probability of the worst pick from the remaining items with flipped signs:
\[\ell(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \sum_{\text{tasks}} \left[ \beta_{j^*_b} - \log\!\!\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}} \exp(\beta_j) \;-\; \beta_{j^*_w} - \log\!\!\!\sum_{j \in \mathcal{S}\setminus\{j^*_b\}} \exp(-\beta_j) \right]\]
We subtract the max before exponentiating (log-sum-exp trick) for numerical stability.


Code
def log_likelihood(beta9):
    beta     = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta9])
    total_ll = 0.0

    for k in range(len(items_arr)):
        idx = items_arr[k]
        b   = best_arr[k]
        w   = worst_arr[k]

        bu = beta[idx]
        m  = bu.max()
        total_ll += (beta[b] - m) - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(bu - m)))

        rem = idx[idx != b]
        wu  = -beta[rem]
        m2  = wu.max()
        total_ll += (-beta[w] - m2) - np.log(np.sum(np.exp(wu - m2)))

    return total_ll


print(f"LL at all-zeros (random guessing): {log_likelihood(np.zeros(9)):.2f}")
print(f"Expected random baseline: {-len(tasks_df)*(np.log(4)+np.log(3)):.2f}")


LL at all-zeros (random guessing): -1689.74
Expected random baseline: -1689.74




Code
result = minimize(lambda b: -log_likelihood(b), np.zeros(9),
                  method="L-BFGS-B", options={"maxiter": 2000, "ftol": 1e-10})

print(f"Optimization converged: {result.success}")
print(f"Log-likelihood at MLE:  {-result.fun:.2f}")

beta_hat9 = result.x
from scipy.optimize import approx_fprime

def neg_ll(b):
    return -log_likelihood(b)

eps = 1e-4
n = len(beta_hat9)
hess = np.zeros((n, n))
for i in range(n):
    e = np.zeros(n)
    e[i] = eps
    grad_plus  = approx_fprime(beta_hat9 + e, neg_ll, eps)
    grad_minus = approx_fprime(beta_hat9 - e, neg_ll, eps)
    hess[i] = (grad_plus - grad_minus) / (2 * eps)

se9 = np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(hess)))
beta_hat  = np.concatenate([[0.0], beta_hat9])
se_full   = np.concatenate([[np.nan], se9])


Optimization converged: True
Log-likelihood at MLE:  -1572.73




Code
def softmax(v):
    v = np.array(v, dtype=float)
    v = v - v.max()
    e = np.exp(v)
    return e / e.sum()

mle_df = pd.DataFrame({

    "beta":  beta_hat,
    "se":    se_full,
    "share": shares_mle,
})

mle_df = mle_df.sort_values("share", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

out = mle_df[["mle_rank","short_name","beta","se","share"]].copy()

y_pos = range(len(mle_df))
ax.barh(list(y_pos), mle_df["share"].values, color="steelblue", height=0.6)

The MLE ranking agrees closely with the counts ranking at the top and bottom. Marketing Analytics has by far the largest share (~28%), nearly 2.5× the next-best class. Analytics Consulting has the smallest share. Some middle-tier courses shift slightly in rank because MNL uses information from all shown-but-not-chosen items, not just the picks. The standard errors are reassuringly small for the top and bottom items, wider for the middle pack.
The shares of preference are easier to interpret than raw \(\hat\beta\)’s: they answer “if all 10 classes were shown on one screen, what fraction of respondents would pick each one as best?”

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
MNL via Bayesian Estimation
We fit the same MNL model using a Metropolis-Hastings random-walk sampler. Instead of a single point estimate, we get a full posterior distribution over \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\).
The posterior is:
\[\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \text{data}) \propto L(\boldsymbol{\beta}) \cdot \pi(\boldsymbol{\beta})\]
We use a weakly informative prior: \(\beta_j \sim N(0, 10)\) for each of the 9 free parameters (SD \(\approx 3.16\)). This is very diffuse relative to the scale of our estimates, so the posterior will be dominated by the data.
The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm proposes a random step from the current parameter values, computes the log-posterior ratio, and accepts or rejects according to that ratio. This produces a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the posterior.


Code
def log_prior(beta9):
    return np.sum(norm.logpdf(beta9, loc=0, scale=np.sqrt(10)))

def log_posterior(beta9):
    return log_likelihood(beta9) + log_prior(beta9)


def run_mh(start, n_iter, step_size):
    K        = len(start)
    draws    = np.zeros((n_iter, K))
    current  = start.copy()
    lp_cur   = log_posterior(current)
    n_accept = 0

    for t in range(n_iter):
        proposal  = current + np.random.normal(0, step_size, size=K)
        lp_prop   = log_posterior(proposal)
        log_ratio = lp_prop - lp_cur
        if np.log(np.random.uniform()) < log_ratio:
            current  = proposal
            lp_cur   = lp_prop
            n_accept += 1
        draws[t] = current

    return draws, n_accept / n_iter


np.random.seed(123)
n_iter    = 10000
step_size = 0.08

print(f"Running MH sampler for {n_iter} iterations, step size = {step_size} ...")
draws, accept_rate = run_mh(beta_hat9, n_iter, step_size)
print(f"Acceptance rate: {accept_rate:.1%}  (target: 25–40%)")

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Comparing the Three Methods

The three methods agree strongly on the top and bottom of the ranking: Marketing Analytics is #1 in all three, and Analytics Consulting is last in all three. The middle of the distribution sees some rank swaps — mostly between courses with similar estimated utilities, where small modeling differences can flip adjacent positions.
The MNL adds over counts by using competitive context. Every time a class is shown alongside others and not chosen, that’s information the counts method ignores. MNL uses it, which is why some middle-tier courses shift rank.
Bayes adds over MLE by giving us credible intervals on the shares of preference directly — we just take percentiles of the softmax-transformed MCMC draws. With MLE we would need the delta method to propagate uncertainty through the softmax, which requires additional computation and is an approximation. Bayes also provides a natural framework for extending the model hierarchically to individual-level preferences.

title: MaxDiff Analysis of MSBA Class Preferences
text:
Discussion
What the data say: Marketing Analytics (MGTA 495) is the most preferred course by a wide margin — its share of preference (~29%) is more than twice that of the second-ranked course. Business Analytics and Customer Analytics cluster in the middle. Analytics Consulting and Mktg/Fin/Ops are the least preferred. The result is somewhat surprising given that Customer Analytics and SQL might be expected to top a “practical skills” ranking; the strong preference for Marketing Analytics may reflect its reputation or the instructor effect.
When to use each method:

Counts is the right tool for a quick executive summary or dashboard. It requires no modeling assumptions, is easy to explain to any audience, and runs in seconds. The trade-off is that it ignores competitive context and gives no principled uncertainty estimates.
MLE MNL is appropriate when you need a single rigorous point estimate with classical standard errors — for example, to report in a paper or a business deliverable. It extracts more information from the data than counts and puts results on a proper probability scale.
Bayesian MNL is best when you need uncertainty on derived quantities (like shares of preference or market simulations), when you plan to extend the model (e.g., hierarchical MNL for individual-level preferences), or when you want to incorporate prior knowledge. The cost is computational — MCMC is slower than optimization.

Caveats: This survey was taken by a self-selected sample of MSBA students, likely biased toward students who were engaged enough to complete it. Preferences may differ by cohort year, prior work experience, and stage in the program. Students who have already taken a course may rate it differently than those who haven’t.
Next steps: With more time, I would fit a hierarchical MNL (mixed logit) to estimate individual-level \(\beta\)’s and see whether there are meaningful clusters of students with different preference profiles. I would also investigate whether preferences differ by professional background or year in the program.

title: S-Mobile: Predicting Customer Churn
text:
Business Problem
S-Mobile, a leading Singapore telecom with approximately 1 million subscribers, faced a 2% monthly churn rate. The traditional response — waiting for customers to call in and threaten to leave — was reactive and trained customers to game the system for discounts.
The goal was to build a proactive churn management system: predict which customers are likely to leave before they do, identify the root causes, design targeted interventions, and evaluate the economics of each action.

title: S-Mobile: Predicting Customer Churn
text:
Methodology

Data & Setup

39,000 training observations + 30,000 representative sample (2% real-world churn rate)
Features: device characteristics, usage behavior (minutes, overage, dropped calls), customer demographics (occupation, credit rating, tenure), service history
Key modeling challenge: training data was balanced at 50% churn for model fitting, then predictions were probability-corrected back to the true 2% population rate for downstream CLV analysis



Step 1 — Churn Prediction Model
Built and compared two models:



Model
Validation AUC




Logistic Regression (final)
~0.70


Random Forest (tuned, RandomizedSearchCV)
~0.695



Random Forest did not materially outperform Logistic Regression on the validation set, suggesting the data has limited nonlinear structure. Logistic Regression was selected as the final model for its interpretability and equivalent predictive performance. Variable car was dropped due to consistent statistical insignificance.


Step 2 — Key Churn Drivers
Using Permutation Importance and Partial Dependence Plots, the top 5 churn drivers identified were:







Driver
Finding




Occupation
Students churn at far higher rates than retired customers


Equipment age (eqpdays)
Older devices strongly predict switching behavior


Overage usage
High overage minutes signal plan mismatch and billing frustration


Credit rating
Low-credit customers are significantly less stable


Tenure (months)
Longer-tenure customers are much less likely to churn





Step 3 — Retention Actions
Five targeted interventions were designed based on the churn drivers, each applied only to high-risk customers in the relevant segment:

Early device upgrade program — for high-risk customers with handsets above 75th percentile age
Plan optimization — for high-risk customers with consistently high overage usage
Student retention offer — flexible plans for students with above-median churn probability
Credit auto-pay incentive — for low-credit customers with high predicted churn risk
Service quality improvement — for high-risk customers experiencing frequent dropped calls



Step 4 — Quantifying Churn Reduction
Using model-based counterfactual predictions on the representative sample (baseline churn rate = 1.99%):



Intervention
Churn Rate Reduction




Credit auto-pay enrollment
−0.88 pp


Early device upgrade
−0.35 pp


Plan optimization
−0.31 pp


Student retention offer
−0.04 pp

−0.02 pp

CLV Economics (5-Year, 10% Annual Discount Rate)
Baseline assumptions: $40/month revenue per customer, 2% monthly churn, 60-month window.

All three interventions generate positive economic returns under realistic cost assumptions. Credit auto-pay delivers the highest leverage — a $258 CLV buffer against a $40–$60 incentive cost.

title: S-Mobile: Predicting Customer Churn
text:
Business Insights
1. Reactive churn management is inferior. The model-based proactive approach targets customers before they decide to leave, when retention offers are more effective and less expensive.
2. Not all interventions are equal. Credit auto-pay delivers 3× the CLV impact of plan optimization. Prioritizing interventions by economic return — not just churn reduction — is critical for budget efficiency.
3. Probability correction matters for economics. Predictions from a balanced training set (50% churn) would wildly overstate actual churn risk. Correcting back to the 2% population rate is essential before any CLV or cost-benefit calculation.
4. Targeting beats mass deployment. Applying interventions only to high-risk customers within the relevant driver segment maximizes ROI. For example, offering upgrade incentives to all customers wastes budget on low-risk customers who would have stayed anyway.
5. Model validation should use RCT. The counterfactual estimates provide a sound starting point, but a pilot randomized experiment is needed before large-scale rollout to confirm the real-world churn reductions are statistically significant.

title: Creative Gaming: Uplift Modeling
text:
Business Problem
Creative Gaming needed to decide which of 120,000 customers to show ads for their new game Zalon ($14.99), where each ad costs $1.50 in lost coin purchases. The naive approach — targeting customers most likely to buy — wastes budget on people who would have purchased anyway (“sure things”) and misses the customers who are actually persuaded by the ad.
The key question: which customers’ behavior is genuinely changed by seeing an ad?

title: Creative Gaming: Uplift Modeling
section: Why Uplift Modeling, Not Propensity Modeling?
text:
Why Uplift Modeling, Not Propensity Modeling?
Standard propensity models rank customers by P(purchase | ad shown), which conflates purchase likelihood with ad effectiveness. Uplift modeling instead estimates the incremental causal effect of the ad per customer:
\[\text{Uplift}_i = P(\text{purchase} \mid \text{ad}=1, X_i) - P(\text{purchase} \mid \text{ad}=0, X_i)\]
This separates customers into four behavioral segments: Persuadables (target these), Sure Things (waste of budget), Lost Causes (ignore), and Do-Not-Disturbs (avoid — ads hurt conversion).
The breakeven uplift threshold is: $1.50 / $14.99 ≈ 0.10 — only target customers whose incremental purchase probability exceeds 10%.

title: Creative Gaming: Uplift Modeling
text:
Methodology

Data & Experimental Setup
Creative Gaming’s random email allocation policy had created natural experimental data:

Group 1 (Control): 30,000 customers who received no ad (cg_organic_control)
Group 2 (Treatment): 30,000 randomly selected customers who received the Zalon ad (cg_ad_random)
Combined into a stacked RCT dataset of 60,000 observations with 70/30 train/test split, stratified by converted and ad



Uplift Model Architecture
For each model type, two separate models were trained — one on the treatment group and one on the control group — then the uplift score was computed as the difference in predicted probabilities:







Model
Hyperparameters Tuned




Logistic Regression
Baseline (no tuning needed)


Neural Network (MLP)
Hidden layer size: {(100,), (200,)}; alpha: {1e-6, 1e-4, 1e-3}; learning rate: {1e-3, 5e-4}


Random Forest
n_estimators: {100, 200}; max_depth: {5, 10, None}; min_samples_leaf: {10, 50, 100}


XGBoost
n_estimators: {50, 100, 200}; max_depth: {3, 5, 7}; learning_rate: {0.05, 0.1}; min_child_weight: {1, 5}



All ML models used 5-fold cross-validation for hyperparameter tuning.

Key Results

Uplift vs. Propensity: Targeting the Best 30,000 of 120,000 Customers

Uplift targeting consistently outperformed propensity targeting across all four models. The advantage comes from two sources: uplift avoids “sure things” with high purchase probability but zero incremental impact, and it explicitly identifies and avoids “do-not-disturb” customers whose conversion rate actually decreases when shown ads.


Optimal Targeting Percentage
Rather than arbitrarily targeting 25% (30K of 120K), the optimal targeting proportion was derived using the breakeven condition (uplift ≥ 0.10):

Propensity model (Logistic): optimal ≈ 50% of customers
Uplift model (Logistic): optimal ≈ 15% of customers

The uplift model targets a much smaller, more concentrated group of genuinely persuadable customers — reducing cost while maximizing incremental profit.


What the Uplift Charts Revealed
The uplift bar charts showed that the top 20% of customers had uplift above 20% — highly persuadable segments. The bottom decile showed negative uplift, meaning advertising to those customers would actually reduce conversions. This confirms that a selective targeting strategy is essential.
The correlation analysis further validated the model:

Uplift score and pred_treatment: ρ = +0.55 — customers more likely to respond to ads have higher uplift
Uplift score and pred_control: ρ = −0.66 — customers who would buy anyway have lower uplift, not higher

title: Creative Gaming: Uplift Modeling
text:
Business Insights
1. Propensity models waste money on “sure things.” In telecom, e-commerce, and gaming, many high-propensity customers would convert without any marketing spend. Uplift modeling correctly identifies them as low-priority targets.
2. Do-not-disturb customers are a real cost. Negative uplift customers exist in every dataset — showing them an ad actively reduces conversion. Propensity models cannot detect this; uplift models can.
3. Smaller targeted groups can generate more profit. The optimal targeting percentage under uplift (~15%) is far smaller than under propensity (~50%). Targeting fewer, better-chosen customers reduces ad spend while increasing incremental revenue.
4. RCT data is the gold standard for uplift modeling. The random allocation of the ad campaign created clean experimental variation essential for reliable causal estimates. Without this, uplift scores would be confounded by selection bias.
5. Model complexity matters less than model type. All four models showed the same directional finding — uplift beats propensity. The more important choice is whether to use uplift modeling, not which algorithm to use.

Computed uplift scores, generated uplift tables and incremental uplift plots for all models
Derived the optimal targeting percentage using the breakeven threshold formula for both propensity and uplift approaches
Wrote the conceptual explanation distinguishing the four customer segments (Persuadables, Sure Things, Lost Causes, Do-Not-Disturbs)

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Does raising the minimum wage cause unemployment? Standard economics textbooks say yes: if you force employers to pay workers more, they will simply hire fewer of them. Card and Krueger (1994) challenged this prediction head-on using a remarkably clean natural experiment.
On April 1, 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour — the highest state minimum wage in the country at the time. Pennsylvania, right next door, kept its minimum wage unchanged at $4.25. Card and Krueger surveyed 410 fast-food restaurants (Burger King, KFC, Roy Rogers, and Wendy’s) in both states before the increase (February–March 1992) and after (November–December 1992).
This setup is the classic Difference-in-Differences (DiD) design:

Treatment group: New Jersey restaurants (subject to the wage increase)
Control group: Pennsylvania restaurants (no change)
Key assumption: Without the minimum wage increase, employment trends in both states would have moved in parallel

The DiD estimator subtracts two differences:
\[
\hat{\tau}_{DiD}
=
(\bar{Y}_{NJ,after} - \bar{Y}_{NJ,before})
-
(\bar{Y}_{PA,after} - \bar{Y}_{PA,before})
\]
By comparing the change in NJ to the change in PA, we difference out any seasonal trends or macroeconomic shocks that affected both states equally — leaving only the effect of the minimum wage.
Their headline finding: employment in New Jersey did not fall after the minimum wage increase. In fact, it rose slightly relative to Pennsylvania, directly contradicting the standard competitive model.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
section: Something Additional: Visualizing the Wage Distribution Shift
text:
Something Additional: Visualizing the Wage Distribution Shift
One of the most compelling pieces of evidence in the paper is Figure 1: the distribution of starting wages in NJ and PA before and after the minimum wage increase. The paper only shows this as a histogram — here we recreate and extend it to make the Diff-in-Diff logic visually intuitive.
The key insight: if the minimum wage is truly binding (i.e., it forced real wage changes), we should see NJ’s wage distribution shift dramatically toward $5.05 after April 1992, while PA’s distribution stays flat. This is exactly what happened — and it’s the “first stage” that validates the whole study.





Starting wage distributions before and after New Jersey’s minimum wage increase. The policy dramatically compressed NJ wages upward to the new $5.05 floor, while Pennsylvania’s distribution barely changed.






Share of stores paying exactly $5.05 (new minimum):
  NJ Wave 2: 89.0%  (paper: 85.2%)
  PA Wave 2: 1.4%  (paper:  1.3%)

Share of stores still paying $4.25 (old minimum):
  NJ Wave 1: 32.2%  (paper: 30.5%)
  PA Wave 1: 34.2%  (paper: 32.9%)
  NJ Wave 2: 0.0%  (paper:  0.0%)
  PA Wave 2: 28.2%  (paper: 25.3%)


What this shows:

Before the increase (Wave 1), NJ and PA had nearly identical wage distributions — about 30% of stores in both states paid exactly the old minimum of $4.25/hr. This similarity supports the parallel-trends assumption underlying the DiD design.
After the increase (Wave 2), 85% of NJ stores piled up right at the new $5.05 floor, while Pennsylvania’s distribution barely moved. By Wave 2, zero NJ stores still paid $4.25.
This dramatic shift is the “first stage” of the causal chain: the law actually changed wages, so any subsequent employment effects can be attributed to the policy rather than coincidence.
Despite this large wage shock, NJ employment increased relative to PA — the central paradox that motivated the paper and challenged a generation of economists to rethink the competitive model of the labor market.

title: Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)

title: Pentathlon: Next Product to Buy Modeling
text:
Business Problem
Pentathlon, a multi-department e-commerce sports retailer, was sending promotional emails without a systematic way to decide which department’s message to send each customer. The choices were: Endurance, Strength, Water, Team, Backcountry, Racquet, or no message at all.
A prior RCT revealed a key tension: higher email frequency boosted short-term revenue but significantly increased unsubscribe rates, reducing long-term customer lifetime value. The goal of this project was to move from a one-size-fits-all approach to customer-level personalized messaging that maximizes expected profit.

title: Pentathlon: Next Product to Buy Modeling
text:
Methodology

Data & Setup

600,000 customer–email observations (70/30 train/test split)
Features: demographics (age, gender, income, education, children) + historical purchase frequency across 6 departments
Target: whether the customer made a purchase within 2 days of receiving the email (buyer), and if so, the order size (total_os)



NPTB Framework
For each customer, we estimated the expected profit of sending each of the 7 possible messages:
\[\text{Expected Profit} = P(\text{purchase} \mid \text{message}) \times \hat{\text{order size}} \times 0.4\]
The 0.4 margin reflects a 60% COGS assumption. Each customer was then assigned the message yielding the highest expected profit.


Models Built
We built and compared four model types for predicting purchase probability:








Model
Approach
Test AUC




Logistic Regression (interaction)
Message × customer feature interactions
≈ 0.88


Neural Network (MLP)
Tuned on hidden layer size, alpha
≈ 0.88


Random Forest
Tuned on depth, n_estimators
≈ 0.88


XGBoost
Tuned on learning rate, depth, subsample
≈ 0.88



Key modeling insight: A baseline logistic model (without interaction terms) assigned 100% of customers to the same “endurance” message — no personalization at all. Adding message × feature interactions diversified recommendations across multiple departments, enabling true NPTB modeling.
A separate OLS regression on buyers only estimated conditional order size per message, which was combined with purchase probability to compute expected profit.

title: Pentathlon: Next Product to Buy Modeling
text:
Key Results

Personalization Substantially Outperforms Every Alternative








Strategy
Avg. Expected Profit / Customer
Total Profit (5M customers)




Personalized (XGBoost)
€0.684

Personalization vs. random assignment: +€616K (+22%)
Personalization vs. best single message: +€283K (+9%)
Personalization vs. no message: +€1.27M (+59%)



Message Distribution Shifts When Profit Is the Goal
When optimizing for purchase probability, ~70% of customers were assigned “Endurance” — one message dominated.
When optimizing for expected profit (purchase probability × order size × margin), the distribution became more balanced:

Endurance: ~43%
Backcountry: ~36%
Strength: ~17%

This shift reveals that Backcountry messages, while not the most likely to generate a purchase, tend to generate much larger orders — making them more profitable for a significant segment of customers.


Why XGBoost Was Selected as the Final Model
All four models achieved similar test AUC (~0.88), so AUC alone did not differentiate them. We selected the final model based on personalized expected profit per customer on the test set — XGBoost produced the highest value across all strategies.

title: Pentathlon: Next Product to Buy Modeling
text:
Business Insights
1. Personalization generates real money at scale. A ~9% improvement over the best uniform strategy translates to nearly €300K in additional profit per 5M-customer campaign — a figure that compounds across multiple campaigns per year.
2. Order size matters, not just purchase likelihood. Optimizing on probability alone misses high-value customers who respond to niche categories with large basket sizes (e.g., backcountry gear). The NPTB framework captures this.
3. For some customers, no email is optimal. Including the no-message option in the decision framework prevents over-messaging customers who are unlikely to convert regardless of the department — protecting long-term engagement and LTV.
4. The proposed 50/50 email policy has room to improve. Pentathlon’s proposed new policy (splitting emails equally between the top 2 departments per customer) improves over random, but does not maximize profit. A fully individualized allocation would outperform the fixed split, especially when the gap between the first and second best message is large.

text:

Designed and implemented the full NPTB prediction pipeline including counterfactual message scoring for all 7 message types
Built interaction logistic regression model and identified why baseline model failed to personalize
Engineered the expected profit formula combining purchase probability, order size regression, and margin
Compared all four models on both AUC and expected profit metrics; made final model selection argument
Wrote the policy critique and improvement recommendations

title: Tuango: Targeting Mobile App Messages
text:
Business Problem
Tuango, a Chinese “deal-of-the-day” platform similar to Groupon, ran a karaoke deal campaign by pushing offer messages through its mobile app. Sending messages has a hidden cost of 9 RMB per customer — if a customer receives too many irrelevant offers and blocks future messages, Tuango permanently loses that marketing channel.
After running a test campaign on 20,908 customers, Tuango had 397,252 remaining customers to contact for the rollout. The question: should all of them receive the message, or only those most likely to buy?

title: Tuango: Targeting Mobile App Messages
text:
Methodology

Data & Setup

20,908 test-sample customers used to build and validate the model
397,252 rollout customers for actual deployment
Key features: RFM variables (Recency, Frequency, Monetary), Age, Gender, Music purchase history
Target variable: whether the customer purchased the karaoke deal (buyer)



Step 1 — Preliminary Analysis

Overall response rate in the test sample: ~6.2% of customers purchased
Among buyers, average order size: ~2.7 sessions (30-minute karaoke sessions at 49 RMB each)
Tuango’s fee: 50% of revenue → margin per response = 0.5 × 49 RMB × avg order size



Step 2 — Logistic Regression Model
Built a logistic regression model predicting purchase probability using RFM + demographics:
Key variable importance findings (Permutation Importance):








Variable
Importance
Direction




Music (prior music purchase)
Highest
↑ increases purchase probability


Gender
High
Female > Other > Male


Frequency
Moderate
↑ more past purchases → more likely to buy


Monetary
Moderate
↑ higher spend → more likely to buy


Age
Low-moderate
↑ older → less likely to buy


Recency
Lowest
Less recent → less likely to buy





Step 3 — Order Size Model
Built a linear regression on buyers only to predict order size. Finding: R-squared is very low — the model explains little variation in order size. This means the RFM variables predict whether someone buys well, but not how much they buy once they decide to purchase.


Step 4 — Breakeven Targeting Rule
Calculated the breakeven response rate:
\[\text{Breakeven} = \frac{\text{Cost per message}}{\text{Margin per response}} = \frac{9 \text{ RMB}}{0.5 \times 49 \times \text{avg order size}}\]
Only customers with predicted purchase probability above this breakeven received the message.

text:
Key Results

Projected vs. Realized Performance




Target All

Logit-based targeting delivered 8× more profit and 18× better ROME than mass messaging.
These numbers come from the actual post-rollout data — Tuango contacted all 397,252 customers (to generate evaluation data), allowing a clean comparison of what would have happened under each strategy.


Why the Model Worked
The test sample response rate was ~6.2%, but the model identified a subset of customers with much higher predicted purchase probability. By filtering out low-probability customers, the targeting strategy:

Concentrated messages on customers more likely to buy
Reduced wasted message costs on unlikely buyers
Avoided over-messaging customers who would block future notifications

title: Tuango: Targeting Mobile App Messages
text:
Business Insights
1. The true cost of a message is not zero. The 9 RMB marginal cost accounts for the long-term risk of customers blocking deal messages — losing that channel permanently is far more costly than a single wasted send.
2. RFM variables are highly predictive for deal targeting. Prior music purchase history and gender were the strongest predictors, suggesting that category affinity and demographics drive deal responsiveness more than raw usage frequency.
3. Order size is hard to predict — but that’s okay. The linear regression showed very low R-squared for order size, meaning customers who buy tend to buy similar amounts regardless of their profile. The key lever is correctly predicting who buys, not how much they buy.
4. Mass messaging is a losing strategy at scale. A 3.1% ROME means the campaign barely broke even. At 397,252 customers, the difference between selective and mass targeting was ¥775,710 in additional profit — from the same customer base.
5. Model validation on actual rollout data confirms no overfitting. The realized post-rollout profit and ROME figures matched the projected direction from the test sample, confirming that the logistic regression generalized well to new customers.

Built and interpreted the logistic regression model including Permutation Importance and Partial Dependence Plots for all variables
Built the order size linear regression and explained why low R-squared is expected in this context
Derived the breakeven response rate and implemented the targeting decision rule
Calculated projected and actual profit and ROME for both strategies; created comparison bar charts
